title.en: Keeping time with the skies: Moon phases and calendars

text.en: At the Patang Mahotsav kite festival on Makar Sankranti, Meera sees the Moon shining in the daytime. She thought the Moon appeared only at night. Why was it there?

The Moon does not make its own light; it shines by reflecting sunlight, and half of it is always lit by the Sun.
The Moon goes round the Earth once in about 27.3 days, and we see different amounts of its lit half, called phases.
From new Moon (no lit part visible) the visible part grows through crescent and first quarter to full Moon, then shrinks back.
Waxing means growing and waning means shrinking, and the cycle from one full Moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, so it can be seen at different times, including in the day.
A day is the time Earth takes to spin once, a month follows the Moon's cycle, and a year is the time Earth takes to go round the Sun.
A solar calendar follows the Sun and has a year of about 365.25 days, which is why we add a leap day every four years.
A lunar calendar follows the Moon's phases, so its year has 12 lunar months of about 354 days.
Indian calendars such as the Shaka era are lunisolar: they add an extra month now and then so that festivals stay in the same season.
The Moon's pull, along with the Sun's, causes tides in the ocean, which people used to plan fishing and travel.

problem.en: Why do we have a leap year?

text.en: Earth takes about 365.25 days to go round the Sun.
The extra quarter day adds up to one day every four years.
So February gets a 29th day in a leap year.

why.en: This keeps the calendar in step with the seasons.

prompt.en: Why does the Moon change shape?

requiredIdeas.en: It reflects sunlight and half is always lit.
As it orbits Earth we see different parts of the lit half.

commonMisconceptions.en: The Moon makes its own light.

points.en: The Moon's phases repeat in about 29.5 days.
Solar calendars follow the Sun, lunar follow the Moon, lunisolar mix both.
Leap years keep the calendar aligned with seasons.
